What are the arguments for and against government spying, specifically programs like PRISM and the NSA?

For: machine learning algorithms need lots of data, including data from completely innocent people, in order to establish patterns and profile suspects.

Against: people shouldn't be spied on without giving consent or without a compelling reason.

For: A (false) sense of security.

Against: It's a violation of the US constitution's fourth amendment limitations on warrantless searches. There is no liberty without privacy. A few intelligence agencies and their corporate contractors are trying to deprive the American people of liberty so they can make a buck. It's among the least American or patriotic things I can think of.

The primary problem with government access to our personal lives is not how they might use it to stop crime now. I have no doubt that for some time, we would see drops in crime.

The problem comes when "crime" gets redefined. What happens when being a member of the minority political party becomes a crime? Or protesting government policy?

Hell, what happens if an incumbent finds himself in a close political race but is able to dig up dirt on his opponent using government surveillance? Or on politically active citizens? Don't you think MLK would have been the victim of a smear campaign if it were possible (I'm SURE we could have dug something up with complete access).

We would see those in power gain an unbreakable grasp on power. Those that ran against them would be destroyed as well as those who sought to expose this phenomenon.

A long time ago we learned that the safety obtained from powerful Governments is transient while the downsides are permanent. Surveillance leads to incredible power, which inevitably leads to abuse.

Never forget: far more people have been killed by their own Governments than all the other sources of murder put together.

Advantages of government (and business) spying.

  1. You are never alone. You can always say "Hi NSA," and know there is a friendly person or AI device listening intently.

  2. Once you've said a few subversive things, you are free to say anything you want as the damage has been done. This type of freedom is soul-liberating.

  3. You no longer have to spend more time reading TOS every time you go to a new website. Now, instead of spending 95 percent of your time reviewing your rights (we all do read all of those, don't we?) and five percent of time reading what you want to, you can spend most of your time reading the fun stuff.

  4. No more frustrating hours of wondering about Adobe Supercookies, NSA Keys, third party cookies, and the list goes on and on. Much time saved.

  5. You can use your leaked or "hacked" medical information for sympathy, rather than just suffering from your debilitating conditions. This is especially good for people with mental illnesses.

Look, the spying is everywhere, but is it used for good or for evil?

Say your iPhone is stolen. Will law enforcement work with Apple and the carriers to recover it? Nope, not at all. Theft is good for industry (and especially insurance) because it means you have to buy a new one.

I had an interesting idea at one point.

  • Fit the reflectors in the center of the road with somewhat powerful RFID chips (range is preferably 1 lane minimum in all horizontal directions).
  • Imprint an encrypted key & the GPS coordinates into the chip (to prevent spoofing).
  • Fit cars with the necessary EM technology to power said RFID chips (since they run off of radio waves IIRC).
  • Have one of these every 5-10 reflectors (it's a lot, but not that much, I think). Whatever is necessary to keep good GPS navigation.

Bam. Your car can know exactly where you are without a GPS, rain, sleet, or night. Very useful for smart self-driving cars as well. You wouldn't have to worry so much about weather, but just regular obstacles at that point (animals, other cars, construction, etc.)

I just don't know the efficacy of an RFID chip that powerful. I know most have very small ranges so that they can be easily powered by low emitting radios. Stores use them IIRC to keep up with inventory and prevent theft?

If we can get wireless charging right, then I feel we should be able to extend the range of RFID chips if that's a problem.
